The comparative method establishes genetic relationship through regular, recurrent sound correspondences, while calquing transfers a grammatical pattern from one language to another without transferring phonological material; a diagnosis anchored in recurrent sound matches and a mode of transfer that carries no phonological material whatever cannot both be true. Philological work has an object of its own: dated written records fix the earliest attestation of a grammatical feature in a language's history. Where the reconstructed history and the documentary record converge on a date later than the separation of the two languages, the ancestral account falls away and transfer remains the only available history. Because Albanian, Romanian, and Bulgarian alike place the definite article after the noun, there is clear indication that the Balkan Sprachbund comprises Albanian, Romanian, Greek, Bulgarian, and Macedonian. The shared features of the Balkan languages are inherited directly from Proto-Indo-European; yet that genealogical account cannot be squared with the composition of the convergence area just described, whose members are drawn from branches far too distantly related for such traits to have survived in common. Adjudication, then, rests not on the striking resemblance itself but on the joint testimony of reconstruction, dated attestation, and areal distribution."
